theme: Be not silent, O God of my praise, the cry against the wicked
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 109. This is the most severe of the imprecatory psalms. Read it carefully, ask whose voice is speaking in the middle section, and watch how the psalm ends.
settingTheScene: Psalm 109 is a psalm of David, and the psalmist is the target of slander and false accusation. He prays against a particular enemy with one of the longest curses in the Bible. Interpreters differ on whether verses 6 to 19 are the psalmist’s curse or a quotation of what his enemies say about him. Whichever reading is taken, the psalm shows what to do with the deepest anger: bring it to God.
observation: “Be not silent, O God of my praise!” (v. 1).
“For wicked and deceitful mouths are opened against me, speaking against me with lying tongues” (v. 2).
“In return for my love they accuse me, but I give myself to prayer” (v. 4).
“So they reward me evil for good, and hatred for my love” (v. 5).
The long curse: “May his days be few; may another take his office” (vv. 6-19).
“But you, O GOD my Lord, deal on my behalf for your name’s sake; because your steadfast love is good, deliver me!” (v. 21).
“For I am poor and needy, and my heart is stricken within me” (v. 22).
“For he stands at the right hand of the needy, to save him from those who condemn his soul to death” (v. 31).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with a plea for God not to be silent. The psalmist has been slandered. The attack is cruel because it is unprovoked: “In return for my love they accuse me.” His response is not to retaliate but to pray: “I give myself to prayer.” The Hebrew is literally, “I am prayer.” His whole life has become an act of prayer in the face of attack.

The long section in verses 6 to 19 is severe. The language is of a legal curse on a specific person: may he be condemned, may his prayer be counted as sin, may his children be fatherless. Many readers find this unsettling, and it is. Some scholars suggest that verses 6 to 19 are a quotation of the accusers’ words against the psalmist, which he then answers beginning in verse 21. In that reading, he is quoting their curses and handing them to God. Others understand the section as his own prayer against an unrepentant persecutor. In either case, the psalm shows what the Bible allows: raw honesty before God about injustice.

Whatever one concludes, the key move is what the psalmist does next. He does not stop with the curse. He turns to God: “But you, O GOD my Lord, deal on my behalf for your name’s sake.” He appeals not to his own righteousness but to God’s name and steadfast love. “Because your steadfast love is good, deliver me!” He admits that he is “poor and needy.” He is desperate.

The psalm ends with confidence and praise: “With my mouth I will give great thanks to the LORD.” He will praise in the midst of the throng. The reason is verse 31: God “stands at the right hand of the needy.” Where an accuser stands at the right hand of the wicked (v. 6), God stands at the right hand of the poor, as an advocate.

The psalm shows us that we may bring even our darkest feelings to God, and that he will turn them toward trust.
connection: Peter quotes verse 8 in Acts 1:20 in connection with Judas, and the early church read this psalm as a picture of the suffering of Christ. Jesus was repaid with hatred for his love (John 15:25). On the cross he prayed for his enemies (Luke 23:34). He is the one who stands at the right hand of God as our advocate (Acts 7:56; 1 John 2:1). Romans 12:14 says, “Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse.”
application:
If you have a bitter feeling against someone, bring it to God in prayer, not into action.

Remember that God stands at the right hand of the needy, as your advocate.

Pray for an enemy by name, for their repentance and their good.
prayerPrompts: Bring God the accusations or hurts you carry, and give yourself to prayer.
Ask him to deal for you for his name’s sake.
Pray for the one who wronged you, as Jesus did.
